```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)
set.seed(258)

normal_pdf <- function(x) dnorm(x)
t_pdf <- function(x, df) dt(x, df)

tail_plot <- function(stat = 1.8, dist = "z", df = 12, alternative = "greater",
                      title = "Reference distribution") {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)
  y <- if (dist == "z") normal_pdf(x) else t_pdf(x, df)
  stat_abs <- abs(stat)
  shade <- switch(
    alternative,
    greater = x >= stat,
    less = x <= stat,
    two = abs(x) >= stat_abs
  )
  p <- plot_ly(width = 620, height = 230) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = if (dist == "z") "N(0,1)" else paste0("t(", df, ")")) |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade], y = y[shade], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.32)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.9)", width = 1),
              name = "p-value area") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = TRUE,
                   zerolinecolor = "#222", zerolinewidth = 1,
                   range = c(-4, 4), fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28),
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
  p
}

# Chi-square reference distribution with a shaded tail (for variance tests)
chisq_tail_plot <- function(stat, df, alternative = "greater",
                            title = "Chi-square reference") {
  x <- seq(0, qchisq(0.999, df), length.out = 500)
  y <- dchisq(x, df)
  shade <- if (alternative == "less") x <= stat else x >= stat
  plot_ly(width = 620, height = 230) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = paste0("chi^2(", df, ")")) |>
    add_trace(x = x[shade], y = y[shade], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.32)",
              line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.9)", width = 1),
              name = "p-value area") |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
      xaxis = list(title = "", zeroline = TRUE, zerolinecolor = "#222",
                   rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28),
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

# Interactive dropdown: switch the shaded p-value area between the three alternatives
pvalue_dropdown <- function(stat = 1.3) {
  x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 600)
  y <- dnorm(x)
  left_idx  <- x <= -abs(stat)
  right_idx <- x >=  abs(stat)
  fill_col <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.55)"
  line_col <- "rgba(249,168,37,0.95)"
  ttl <- function(t) list(text = t, x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15))
  plot_ly(width = 1040, height = 340) |>
    add_lines(x = x, y = y, line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4),
              name = "N(0,1)", hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[left_idx], y = y[left_idx], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_col,
              line = list(color = line_col, width = 1),
              name = "left tail", visible = FALSE, hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    add_trace(x = x[right_idx], y = y[right_idx], type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
              fill = "tozeroy", fillcolor = fill_col,
              line = list(color = line_col, width = 1),
              name = "right tail", visible = TRUE, hoverinfo = "skip") |>
    layout(
      title = ttl("Right-tailed p-value  (Ha: θ > θ₀)"),
      xaxis = list(title = "test statistic", range = c(-4, 4), zeroline = TRUE,
                   zerolinecolor = "#222", fixedrange = TRUE),
      yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
      margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 70, b = 34),
      showlegend = FALSE,
      updatemenus = list(list(
        type = "dropdown", direction = "down",
        x = 0.985, xanchor = "right", y = 1.16, yanchor = "top",
        bgcolor = "#ffffff", bordercolor = "#00695c",
        buttons = list(
          list(method = "update", label = "Right-tailed  (Ha: >)",
               args = list(list(visible = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)),
                           list(title = ttl("Right-tailed p-value  (Ha: θ > θ₀)")))),
          list(method = "update", label = "Left-tailed  (Ha: <)",
               args = list(list(visible = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)),
                           list(title = ttl("Left-tailed p-value  (Ha: θ < θ₀)")))),
          list(method = "update", label = "Two-tailed  (Ha: ≠)",
               args = list(list(visible = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE)),
                           list(title = ttl("Two-tailed p-value  (Ha: θ ≠ θ₀)"))))
        )
      ))
    ) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
}

```

---

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Logic</span>
Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, and decisions.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">One sample</span>
Tests for one mean, one proportion, and one variance.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two sample</span>
Tests for differences, ratios, and paired data.
:::
::::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Big theme</span>
A hypothesis test asks whether the observed statistic would be surprising if the null hypothesis were true.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Output skill</span>
State the conclusion in context: reject or fail to reject, then translate that decision back to the population parameter.
:::
::::

---

## What a Hypothesis Test Does

::: {.defbox .fragment}
<span class="label">High Level Idea</span>
A hypothesis test uses sample evidence to decide whether there is enough evidence against a claim about a population parameter.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Null hypothesis, $H_0$</span>
The status quo, no-effect, or no-difference claim.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Alternative hypothesis, $H_a$</span>
The direction of evidence we are trying to detect.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The test is performed **assuming $H_0$ is true**. The p-value measures how unusual the data are under that assumption.
:::

---

## The Five-Step Procedure

::: {.slide-stack}
<ol class="step-list">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>1. Choose $\alpha$.</strong> Set the significance level before making the decision.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>2. State hypotheses.</strong> Use the correct population parameter.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>3. Compute statistic.</strong> Standardize the estimate with the correct standard error.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>4. Find the p-value.</strong> Use the tail area that matches $H_a$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>5. Conclude.</strong> Compare to $\alpha$ and write the conclusion in context.</li>
</ol>

::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
tail_plot(stat = 1.55, alternative = "greater",
          title = "P-value area")
```
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Step 4 and Step 5 are separate: first calculate evidence, then make the decision.
:::
:::

---

## Choosing the Alternative

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Left-tailed</span>
$$H_a:\theta < \theta_0$$
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter decreased or is smaller.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Right-tailed</span>
$$H_a:\theta > \theta_0$$
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter increased or is larger.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Two-sided</span>
$$H_a:\theta \ne \theta_0$$
Use when the research question asks whether the parameter changed in either direction.
:::
::::

---

## P-Value Areas

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
<ol class="step-list compact-steps">
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Left-tailed:</strong> $P(T \le t^*)$ or $P(Z \le z^*)$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Right-tailed:</strong> $P(T \ge t^*)$ or $P(Z \ge z^*)$.</li>
  <li class="fragment"><strong>Two-sided:</strong> double the matching one-tail area.</li>
</ol>
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
Use the **dropdown** at the top-right of the plot to switch the shaded p-value area between the three alternative hypotheses.
:::
:::
::::

::: {.dropdown-plot}
```{r}
pvalue_dropdown(stat = 1.3)
```
:::

---

## Decision Rule

::: {.slide-stack}
::: {.decision-cards}
::: {.defbox}
<span class="label">If p-value $\le \alpha$</span>
Reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a$.
:::

::: {.defbox}
<span class="label">If p-value $> \alpha$</span>
Fail to reject $H_0$.
:::
:::

::: {.warnbox}
<span class="label">Careful language</span>
Failing to reject $H_0$ does **not** prove $H_0$. It only means the sample does not provide enough evidence against it at the chosen significance level.
:::

::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
tail_plot(stat = 2.05, alternative = "greater",
          title = "Small p-value: evidence against H0")
```
:::
:::

---

## Reading Strength of Evidence

::: {.evidence-layout}
::: {.table-gap}
| p-value range | Textbook language |
|---|---|
| $\le 0.001$ | Very strong evidence against $H_0$ |
| $0.001$ to $0.01$ | Strong evidence |
| $0.01$ to $0.05$ | Evidence |
| $0.05$ to $0.075$ | Some evidence |
| $0.075$ to $0.10$ | Slight evidence |
| $>0.10$ | Little or no evidence against $H_0$ |
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .table-note}
Statistical significance does not measure practical importance. Pair the p-value with an estimate or confidence interval.
:::
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A test gives p-value $0.032$ and uses $\alpha=0.05$. What should we do?
::::

- Fail to reject $H_0$
- [Reject $H_0$]{.correct data-explanation="Because 0.032 is less than 0.05, the result is statistically significant at the 5% level."}
- Prove $H_0$ is false
- Increase $\alpha$ until the test works

---

## One Mean, Known $\sigma$

::: {.defbox}
When the population standard deviation is known, use a standard normal reference distribution:

$$
z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$Z\sim N(0,1)$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use when</span>
Testing a population mean with known $\sigma$ and an appropriate random/normal-or-large-sample setup.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Coffee Fill Volume

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
The cafe chain **Steeped** advertises that a large iced latte is filled to a target of $\mu_0=7.2$ oz of base. Customers complain the cups feel light, so quality control pulls a random sample of $n=40$ cups.

From years of calibration records, the filling machine's standard deviation is known: $\sigma=1.1$ oz. The sample mean is $\bar{x}=6.7$ oz.

Test whether the true mean fill volume has **dropped below** 7.2 oz at $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$
H_0:\mu=7.2
\qquad
H_a:\mu<7.2
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot}
```{r}
tail_plot(stat = -2.8748, alternative = "less",
          title = "Coffee example: left-tailed z test")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Coffee Example: Calculation

::: {.examplebox}
$$
z^*=\frac{6.7-7.2}{1.1/\sqrt{40}}=-2.8748
$$

$$
\text{p-value}=P(Z\le -2.8748)=0.00202
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
$0.00202 \le 0.05$, so reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Conclusion</span>
There is sufficient evidence that the mean large-coffee fill volume is below 7.2 oz.
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Coffee z Test

```{webr}
n <- 40
xbar <- 6.7
mu0 <- 7.2
sigma <- 1.1

z_star <- (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))
p_value <- pnorm(z_star)

z_star
p_value
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In the coffee example, the alternative is $H_a:\mu<7.2$. Which p-value formula matches the test?
::::

- $P(Z\ge z^*)$
- [$P(Z\le z^*)$]{.correct data-explanation="A less-than alternative is left-tailed, so the p-value is the area to the left of the observed z statistic."}
- $2P(Z\ge z^*)$
- $P(Z=z^*)$

---

## One Mean, Unknown $\sigma$

::: {.defbox}
When $\sigma$ is unknown, replace it with $s$ and use the Student $t$ distribution:

$$
t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$t$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>
Random/independent observations; population normal or sample large enough for the $t$ approximation.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Food Delivery ETA

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
The delivery app **DashEats** promises an average drop-off time of $16.5$ minutes. Suspecting orders really take longer, a student logs the wait (in minutes) on 12 random orders:

`16.2, 18.4, 15.7, 19.1, 17.3, 16.9, 20.4, 18.2, 15.9, 17.6, 16.7, 19.8`

Test whether the true mean delivery time is **greater** than the advertised 16.5 minutes.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\mu=16.5,\qquad H_a:\mu>16.5$$
$\sigma$ is unknown, so use a one-sample $t$ test.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
tail_plot(stat = 2.682, dist = "t", df = 11, alternative = "greater",
          title = "Right-tailed t test, df = 11")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Wait-Time t Test

```{webr}
waits <- c(16.2, 18.4, 15.7, 19.1, 17.3, 16.9,
           20.4, 18.2, 15.9, 17.6, 16.7, 19.8)

t.test(waits, alternative = "greater", mu = 16.5)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The output gives $t=2.682$, $df=11$, and p-value $0.0107$. At $\alpha=0.05$, reject $H_0$.
:::

---

## One Proportion Test

::: {.defbox}
For a test about one population proportion $p$:

$$
z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Use the null value</span>
The standard error uses $p_0$, not $\hat p$.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Large-count check</span>
Under $H_0$, both $np_0$ and $n(1-p_0)$ should be at least 10.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Reusable Cup Discount

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
Last year only $10\%$ of students used the reusable-cup discount at a campus cafe. After a sustainability campaign, a fresh random survey finds $x=68$ of $n=520$ students bringing their own cup.

Is this evidence that the participation rate has **increased** above $10\%$?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:p=0.10,\qquad H_a:p>0.10$$

$$\hat p=\frac{68}{520}=0.1308$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
tail_plot(stat = 2.34, alternative = "greater",
          title = "Right-tailed z test for a proportion")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: One Proportion

```{webr}
x <- 68
n <- 520
p0 <- 0.10

phat <- x / n
z_star <- (phat - p0) / sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
p_value <- 1 - pnorm(z_star)

phat
z_star
p_value

prop.test(x, n, p = p0, alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

For the recycling test, why is the alternative $H_a:p>0.10$?
::::

- The sample proportion is always greater than the null value
- [The research question asks whether participation has increased]{.correct data-explanation="An increase means the population proportion is larger than the old value 0.10, so the test is right-tailed."}
- The sample size is greater than 30
- Proportion tests are always right-tailed

---

## One Variance Test

::: {.defbox}
For one normal population, test a variance using the chi-square statistic:

$$
\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$\chi^2$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Important condition</span>
The population should be approximately normal. Variance tests are sensitive to non-normality.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Protein Scoop Consistency

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
A fitness brand claims its protein powder is dosed so precisely that scoop weights have standard deviation at most $2.8$ g. A reviewer weighs a random sample of $n=28$ scoops and finds $s=3.4$ g.

Does this **undermine** the consistency claim? Use $\alpha=0.05$ and assume scoop weights are normal.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\sigma^2=2.8^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma^2>2.8^2$$

A larger sample spread is evidence against the "at most 2.8 g" claim.
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
chisq_tail_plot(stat = 39.81, df = 27, alternative = "greater",
                title = "Right-tailed chi-square test, df = 27")
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Scoop Variance Test

```{webr}
n <- 28
s <- 3.4
sigma0 <- 2.8

chi_star <- (n - 1) * s^2 / sigma0^2
p_value <- 1 - pchisq(chi_star, df = n - 1)

chi_star
p_value
```

---

## Two-Sample Test Targets

| Target parameter | Typical question | Reference distribution |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu_1-\mu_2$ | Are two population means different? | $Z$ or $t$ |
| $p_1-p_2$ | Are two population proportions different? | $Z$ |
| $\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2$ | Are two population variances different? | $F$ |
| $\mu_d$ | Is the mean paired difference nonzero? | $t$ |

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .spaced-note}
Start by deciding whether the samples are independent or paired. That choice changes the whole test.
:::

---

## Two Means: Known $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$

::: {.defbox}
When both population standard deviations are known:

$$
z^*=
\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}
{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
Usually $D_0=0$ when testing whether the population means are equal.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
Use $Z$ because the population standard deviations are known.
:::
::::

---

## Two Means: Unknown Variances

::: {.defbox}
For unequal or unspecified population variances, use Welch's two-sample $t$ test:

$$
t^*=
\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}
{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Default</span>
Welch is a good default when equal variances are not clearly justified.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Degrees of freedom</span>
Software uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Active Recall vs Rereading

::: {.examplebox}
Decades of memory research suggest **active recall** (self-testing) beats passively rereading notes. Two independent tutorial sections each prepare with one method, then write the same quiz.

Active recall: `88 91 85 94 89 90 87 92 86 93 89 90`
Rereading: `84 86 82 88 85 83 81 87 84 86`

Does active recall produce a higher mean quiz score?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Let $\mu_1$ be the active-recall mean and $\mu_2$ the rereading mean. Test $H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0$ against $H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0$.
:::

---

## Check in R: Two-Sample t Test

```{webr}
active <- c(88, 91, 85, 94, 89, 90, 87, 92, 86, 93, 89, 90)
review <- c(84, 86, 82, 88, 85, 83, 81, 87, 84, 86)

t.test(active, review, alternative = "greater", var.equal = FALSE)
```

---

## Difference of Proportions

::: {.defbox}
When testing $H_0:p_1-p_2=0$, pool the sample proportions under the null:

$$
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}
$$

$$
z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}
{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}
$$
:::

---

## Example: Push Notifications

::: {.examplebox}
A habit-tracking app runs an experiment: half of new users get a daily push notification, half get none. For each user the app records whether they completed a workout that day.

Push notification: $142$ check-ins out of $360$ users
No notification: $118$ check-ins out of $370$ users

Test whether the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$
H_0:p_1-p_2=0,\qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0
$$
:::

---

## Check in R: Two Proportions

```{webr}
successes <- c(142, 118)
totals <- c(360, 370)

prop.test(successes, totals, alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The output gives p-value about $0.0166$, so there is evidence that reminder texts increase the sign-up rate.
:::

---

## Ratio of Variances

::: {.defbox}
For two normal populations, test a ratio of variances with

$$
F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
$$

using an $F$ reference distribution with $n_1-1$ and $n_2-1$ degrees of freedom.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Normality matters</span>
The $F$ test for variances is sensitive to non-normality.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Two-sided idea</span>
Extreme ratios in either direction count as evidence against equal variances.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Streaky Scorer

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.examplebox}
Two basketball players average about the same points per game, but a scout suspects **Player A is streakier** — more variable game to game.

Player A: `78 85 72 91 68 88 75 82 95 70 84 77`
Player B: `82 84 79 85 81 83 80 86 82 84`

Test whether Player A has the larger scoring variance at $\alpha=0.05$.
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
$$H_0:\sigma_A^2=\sigma_B^2,\qquad H_a:\sigma_A^2>\sigma_B^2$$

$$F^*=\frac{s_A^2}{s_B^2}\sim F_{n_A-1,\,n_B-1}$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.mini-plot .fragment}
```{r}
fx <- seq(0, 6, length.out = 500)
plot_ly(width = 620, height = 230) |>
  add_lines(x = fx, y = df(fx, 11, 9),
            line = list(color = "#1f4e79", width = 4), name = "F(11, 9)") |>
  add_trace(x = fx[fx >= 3.1], y = df(fx[fx >= 3.1], 11, 9),
            type = "scatter", mode = "lines", fill = "tozeroy",
            fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.32)",
            line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.9)", width = 1)) |>
  layout(title = list(text = "Right-tailed F test, df = 11, 9",
                      x = 0.02, font = list(size = 15)),
         xaxis = list(title = "", fixedrange = TRUE, zeroline = TRUE,
                      zerolinecolor = "#222"),
         yaxis = list(title = "", rangemode = "tozero", fixedrange = TRUE),
         margin = list(l = 42, r = 12, t = 36, b = 28), showlegend = FALSE) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE, responsive = TRUE)
```
:::
:::
::::

---

## Check in R: Ratio of Variances

```{webr}
player_a <- c(78, 85, 72, 91, 68, 88, 75, 82, 95, 70, 84, 77)
player_b <- c(82, 84, 79, 85, 81, 83, 80, 86, 82, 84)

var.test(player_a, player_b, alternative = "greater")
```

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
`var.test` reports $F^*$, the two degrees of freedom, and the p-value. An $F^*$ well above 1 is evidence that Player A's scoring is more variable.
:::

---

## Paired Data

::: {.defbox}
For matched pairs or before-after data, first reduce the data to differences:

$$
d_i = \text{new}_i-\text{current}_i
$$

Then run a one-sample $t$ test on $\mu_d$.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Not independent groups</span>
The two measurements inside a pair are linked.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Reference distribution</span>
$t$ with $n-1$ degrees of freedom for the differences.
:::
::::

---

## Example: Pomodoro Focus Timer

::: {.examplebox}
Each of 12 students completes a timed practice set, then writes a comparable set after a week of studying with the **Pomodoro** technique (25-minute focus blocks). Scores are paired within each student.

Before: `34 29 41 38 36 33 40 31 37 35 39 32`
After: `36 31 43 39 38 35 39 34 40 37 41 33`

Can we conclude the technique improves scores?
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Use paired differences $d_i=\text{after}_i-\text{before}_i$ and test $H_0:\mu_d=0$ against $H_a:\mu_d>0$.
:::

---

## Check in R: Paired Pomodoro Test

```{webr}
before <- c(34, 29, 41, 38, 36, 33, 40, 31, 37, 35, 39, 32)
after <- c(36, 31, 43, 39, 38, 35, 39, 34, 40, 37, 41, 33)

t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE, alternative = "greater")
```

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

In the Pomodoro example, why is a paired $t$ test appropriate?
::::

- The two samples have the same mean
- The sample size is less than 30
- [Each student has both before and after scores, so observations are matched within student]{.correct data-explanation="The student creates a natural pair: the before score and after score come from the same person."}
- Proportion tests cannot use score data

---

## Assumptions: Two Independent Means

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, each sample is less than 10% of its population.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Model condition</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Each population is approximately normal, or both sample sizes are large enough for the CLT.</li>
  <li class="fragment">For a pooled test, equal population variances should be reasonable.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Difference of Proportions

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Sampling structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two groups are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.</li>
  <li class="fragment">If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Large-count condition</span>
<p class="fragment">For each group, check successes and failures:</p>

::: {.fragment}
$$
x_i\ge 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_i-x_i\ge 10
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Ratio of Variances

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Required structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The two samples are independent.</li>
  <li class="fragment">Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
<span class="label">Normality matters here</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">The $F$ test for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.</li>
  <li class="fragment">This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based tests.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Assumptions: Paired Data

:::: {.assumption-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Paired structure</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Each pair comes from the same unit, matched units, or a before-after measurement.</li>
  <li class="fragment">The pairs themselves are independent of one another.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Model condition</span>
<ul class="assumption-list">
  <li class="fragment">Analyze the differences $d_i$, not the two original columns separately.</li>
  <li class="fragment">For small samples, the distribution of differences should be approximately normal.</li>
</ul>
:::
::::

---

## Choosing the Right Test

| If the problem asks for... | Use... |
|---|---|
| one mean and gives $\sigma$ | one-sample $z$ test |
| one mean and gives $s$ or raw data | one-sample $t$ test |
| one proportion | one-proportion $z$ test |
| one variance | chi-square test |
| difference of means, known $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ | two-sample $z$ test |
| difference of means, equal variances | pooled two-sample $t$ test |
| difference of means, unequal/unspecified variances | Welch two-sample $t$ test |
| difference of proportions | two-proportion $z$ test |
| ratio of variances | $F$ test |
| before-after or matched data | paired $t$ test on differences |

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A problem gives raw before-and-after blood pressure measurements on the same 12 patients. Which test should you use?
::::

- Two independent sample $t$ test
- One-proportion $z$ test
- [Paired $t$ test on the differences]{.correct data-explanation="Before-and-after measurements on the same patient are paired. First compute each patient's difference, then use a one-sample t test on those differences."}
- $F$ test for variances

---

## Test Statistic Cheat Sheet

| Situation | Test statistic |
|---|---|
| One mean, $\sigma$ known | $\displaystyle z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$ |
| One mean, $\sigma$ unknown | $\displaystyle t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}$ |
| One proportion | $\displaystyle z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$ |
| One variance | $\displaystyle \chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}$ |
| Difference of proportions | $\displaystyle z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}$ |

---

## What to Write in a Conclusion

:::: {.conclusion-stack}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Decision</span>
Reject or fail to reject $H_0$.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Evidence strength</span>
Use the p-value to describe how strong the evidence is.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Context</span>
Name the population parameter and the direction of the claim.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment .spaced-note}
Good conclusion: "There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill volume for large coffees is below 7.2 oz."
:::
